4a3f068053:
This chapter is about what an architect has to build underneath an LLM system. The goal: six weeks after launch, somebody can answer four questions from evidence. Why was that request slow, what did it cost and who is spending, did quality move, and did any personal data leave the process?

The chapter covers tracing an agent run as one trace, the span attributes and metrics that matter, and propagation across Python, Spring and MCP boundaries. It works through the arithmetic of cardinality, telemetry cost and sampling, and redaction and content-capture policy. Then come SLO burn-rate alerting, cost attribution, cache and latency regressions, online quality signals, drift detection, replay, runaway-loop guards and retention.

Chapter 11 owns evaluation methodology, chapter 12 owns diagnosis and optimisation, and chapter 14 owns the compliance regimes. This chapter produces the data they consume.
dc12a8f57d:
The exam facts in this guide (63 items, 120 minutes, a $175 fee, seven domains with weights of 19, 17, 16, 14, 14, 13 and 7 percent) come from third-party summaries of the CCAR-P blueprint. Treat them as a study map, and check the current official exam guide. The engineering content here doesn't depend on them.

Some product details change quickly: OpenTelemetry GenAI attribute names, Collector processor options, Spring Boot tracing setup, prompt-caching minimums and usage field names, token prices. These are marked check the docs where they appear. Every price, latency, volume and threshold in the examples is an illustrative placeholder, not a measurement of any product.
9a283c8cd4:
An LLM system is observable when every request leaves one trace whose spans carry typed attributes (model, prompt version, token counts by type, cache tokens, cost, tenant, feature), when rates and costs come from unsampled in-process metrics, and when nothing that identifies a person crosses the process boundary unless a written policy says it may.

Everything else, the sampling policy, the alerts, the dashboards, the cost report, the replay set, the drift detectors, is derived from that data and sized against the per-segment targets on the requirements card, with the cost of the telemetry itself on the same page as the cost of the inference.
59181ef444:
Why does this chapter exist? Because most failures of a Claude-based system are invisible to the tools a Spring architect already runs.

  • A fluent wrong answer is an HTTP 200.
  • A prompt edit that moves a timestamp above the cache breakpoint nearly doubles the cost per request (1.93 times in example 10). Not a single status code changes.
  • A tool whose owner added a validation rule makes every request take one extra model call. The error rate stays flat.
  • A new model snapshot behind an alias makes answers a quarter longer. The only symptom is token spend.

Classic request-rate, error-rate and duration dashboards see none of these. So the signals have to be designed in. And they should be designed once, in one wrapper that every model call goes through.
995b805909:
CCAR-P asks about this domain through judgement questions with numbers in them. Costs rose 40 percent after a release, and finance wants the feature responsible. Legal says prompts contain card numbers, and the observability platform may hold none. The observability bill is a third of the inference bill. An alert pages the on-call engineer every afternoon for a latency the SLA permits.

In each case, four answers sound like good practice. One fits the stated constraint at the lowest complexity. The method is the one chapter 01 set up: find the primary requirement, list the hard constraints, eliminate the options that violate them, and prefer the design justified by a measurement.

This chapter supplies the measurements. They all come from one running example, a carrier's customer assistant with three features. So the numbers in section 28 are numbers you've already seen computed.
fd985467fa: A note on scope. This chapter doesn't teach how to build a grader, how to run an A/B test or how to trace a failure down to its root cause. Those are chapters 11 and 12; here you meet only enough of them to see what data they need. Nor does it give legal advice on retention periods or on what counts as personal data. Chapter 14 covers the regimes, and the numbers in section 26 are placeholders for your counsel's answer. What it does cover, in full, is the design of the data those chapters depend on.
97be3032ee: Observability for software was assembled from four older disciplines. Each one answered one failure. Today's LLM-specific practice is those four plus one new problem. Know which piece answers which failure, and the exam's distractors become easy to spot: most wrong answers are a correct tool applied to the wrong failure.
49058eefa7:
The first observability was text. Programs wrote lines to files, and operators ran grep and tail -f. Network gear exposed counters through SNMP, which tools such as MRTG and later Nagios graphed. A telecom architect will remember this layer well: the world of alarms, counters and thresholds.

The model was known failures, watched individually. You decided in advance that disk usage, link errors or process counts mattered, and you set a threshold. That worked while a system was a handful of machines with known failure modes. It stopped working when one user request began to touch dozens of services. No single log file held the story of a request, and no threshold on a single counter explained why that request was slow.
d7537bd95a:
Google's Dapper paper (2010) described the answer. Assign every request an identifier at the edge and pass it through every call. Record a span for each unit of work, with its parent. Reassemble the tree afterwards. Twitter open-sourced Zipkin in 2012 on the same model, and a generation of tracing systems followed.

The deep idea is that the causal structure of a request is data: which call waited on which, which ran in parallel, which retry hid inside which timeout.

Two competing instrumentation standards, OpenTracing and OpenCensus, merged into OpenTelemetry (announced 2019, a CNCF project). It now defines the API, the SDKs, the wire protocol (OTLP) and the Collector. In the Spring world the same ideas arrived as Spring Cloud Sleuth. Spring Boot 3 replaced it with Micrometer Tracing and the Observation API (check the docs for the version you run). Everything in sections 05 to 09 is that lineage applied to a model call.
3c053ed71e:
Site reliability engineering changed what an alert is for, as Google's SRE book (2016) and workbook (2018) describe. A threshold on a symptom pages people for conditions the business doesn't mind.

A service level objective states what the users are promised: "95 percent of requests complete within 7 seconds over 30 days". The complement is an error budget (5 percent). The alert fires on the rate at which the budget is being spent. A burn rate of 1 spends the budget exactly over the window; a burn rate of 6 spends it in five days.

The workbook's multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts use a long window to be sure the burn is real and a short one to be sure it is still happening. Section 16 implements and measures them. The CCAR-P blueprint's emphasis on SLAs in the lifecycle domain, and on monitoring in the evaluation domain, is this tradition written into an exam.
486c755251:
Machine-learning systems added a failure that classical monitoring doesn't have. The service is up, fast and wrong, because the world moved away from the training data.

A practice grew up around it: compare the live input distribution with a reference (population stability index, Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests), track prediction distributions, and sample live cases for labels. That practice is the ancestor of sections 21 and 22. Google's "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems" (2015) argued that monitoring and configuration, not the model, carry most of a production system's cost. That's why this chapter treats the telemetry budget as a first-class requirement.
37082ef6a7:
When teams began shipping language-model features, a wave of LLM-specific tools appeared: prompt logging, trace viewers, evaluation dashboards. The OpenTelemetry project started defining GenAI semantic conventions, standard attribute names such as gen_ai.request.model and gen_ai.usage.input_tokens. At the time of writing these conventions are still marked as in development, so names can change between versions. Check the OpenTelemetry docs and pin the version you follow.

The new problem isn't a missing tool. It's that the most useful debugging data, the prompt and the completion, is also the most dangerous data you hold, because it contains whatever the customer typed. Earlier generations of observability recorded identifiers and numbers. This one is tempted to record conversations. Sections 14, 15 and 26 are about resisting that temptation without losing the ability to debug.
a564861f2d: Five properties of a Claude call make the standard dashboards insufficient. Each one maps to a signal you must add. They're worth stating plainly, because exam scenarios are built on them.
1aa67a9d67:
The failure is a 200. A language model returns a fluent answer whether or not it is right. The wrong amount in a bill explanation, the superseded policy, the refusal that shouldn't have happened: none of them changes a status code. Quality has to be inferred from behavioural proxies (escalation, re-ask, thumbs-down, human override) and from a graded sample (section 21). A sudden change in either is an event.

The unit cost varies per request. A REST call costs roughly the same every time. A model call costs the sum of input tokens, output tokens, cache writes and cache reads, each at a different price. Those numbers move when somebody edits a prompt, when a retrieval step returns twelve chunks instead of eight, or when the model decides to call a tool a second time.

Latency is dominated by tokens, not hops. Time to first token tracks the prefill of the input. Total time tracks the number of output tokens at a decode rate. An agent multiplies both by the number of loop iterations. And the latency the user feels is neither one. It's the time to the first token of the final answer, which includes every step before it (section 05).
e7285c8098:
The prompt is code that changes without a deploy. A template edited in a database, a retrieval index rebuilt overnight, a model alias that moves to a new snapshot: each changes behaviour while the service binary is untouched. So every span and metric carries the prompt version, the model identifier actually returned by the API, and the index version. That way "what changed" has an answer.

The input is the hazard. The data that makes the system debuggable is the customer's own words, account details and sometimes card numbers. The telemetry pipeline is therefore itself a data-processing system in scope for the privacy programme. It carries the same retention, access and erasure obligations as the system of record.
89022db5cb:
Chapter 01 put four numbers on a card. Observability adds its own lines to the same card, written in the same form: literal, per segment, with a percentile or a rate and a measurement window.

The running example for this chapter is a carrier's customer assistant with three features sharing one platform. The card below is what the rest of the chapter is derived from. Every number is an illustrative placeholder; what matters is the form.
7c92e873df:
Four further lines are platform-wide.

  • The telemetry budget: all telemetry lines together (traces, metric series, indexed content, storage) stay under 5 percent of inference spend. This chapter uses that decision rule and defends it with arithmetic in section 12.
  • The privacy rule: zero card numbers or national identifiers in the observability platform, verified by a canary test on every build (example 08). No raw customer identifier appears in any trace or metric.
  • Retention: metrics 13 months, traces 14 days, redacted content 30 days, guardrail-block records 90 days, subject to your counsel (section 26).
  • Attribution: cost and latency can be reported by feature, tenant tier, model and prompt version within five minutes of a request.
4dc07904a3:
Two habits from chapter 01 carry over unchanged.

First, requirements are literal and per segment. "Latency is under 7 seconds" isn't testable. This is: "p95 of bill_explain end-to-end is at most 7.0 seconds, measured over one hour windows, excluding requests that were escalated before the first model call". A single fleet-wide p95 hides a slow feature behind a fast one. That's the telemetry version of the aggregate-gate anti-pattern.

Second, every requirement names the signal that proves it. The root span duration proves the SLA. A derived attribute proves the first-answer-token target (section 05). The canary test proves the privacy rule. Replaying past incidents through the alert catalogue proves the detection-time targets; example 16 does this and prints how long after the start each alert fires. A requirement that nothing measures is a wish.
4e7aecfa67:
Take a single question to an agentic assistant. It produces an input guardrail check, a model call that decides which tools to use, and two tool executions: one a Spring service, one an MCP server across a network boundary. Then a second model call writes the answer, and an output guardrail runs. That's seven spans, two of them model calls. The larger features add a query rewrite, an embedding call, a vector search and a rerank.

Log each model call in isolation and you can read "a Sonnet call took 3.4 seconds and used 2,400 fresh input tokens". You can't tell which request it served, what ran in parallel with it, or whether the request was eventually escalated to a person.

Distributed tracing solves exactly this. You get one trace per user request and one span per step. Parent and child relationships record causality, and a trace identifier is propagated across every process boundary. A Spring architect knows it as what Sleuth, and now Micrometer Tracing, do for service calls. The agent loop is just one more caller in the same graph.
31940cd849: Example 01 builds the tree for the request above, using the wrapper from section 07, and prints it. The numbers are simulated (the clock is virtual), but the structure is the real one. That includes a detail that matters for the critical path. The two tools run in parallel, so the wall time they contribute is the larger of the two, 410 ms, not the sum of 590 ms.
0338794fe5:
Time to first token (TTFT) of one call is the prefill of its input plus one decode step. It grows with the number of fresh (uncached) input tokens, and shrinks when the prompt prefix is served from the cache. The total duration of a call is TTFT plus the output tokens divided by the decode rate.

What the user feels in a streaming interface is a third number, and no single call reports it. It's the time to first answer token, TTFA: the start time of the final model call plus that call's TTFT, measured from the start of the request.

In the agent above, TTFT of the final call is 0.70 s. TTFA is 3.05 s, because the first model call (1.9 s), the tools (0.41 s) and the guardrail all happen first. A dashboard of per-call TTFT shows a healthy 0.7 seconds while customers wait three.
05cfd90bc7:
The distinction decides which fix applies.

  • A slow TTFA caused by a long prefill responds to prompt caching and context trimming (chapter 05).
  • A slow total caused by long answers responds to shorter outputs, a smaller model, or streaming so the wait is hidden.
  • A slow TTFA caused by an extra loop iteration responds to neither. It needs the tool fixed (section 20).

So the requirements card in section 04 states both a total p95 and a TTFA p95 per feature. The wrapper records the first-token time on every chat span, so TTFA can be derived from the tree. Example 12 computes all three for each feature over 60,000 synthetic requests.
d4ea4bebdb: An observability project is tempted to start from what the tools can collect. Start from the questions instead. Each row below is a question somebody will ask within a quarter of launch, the signal that answers it, and where the signal comes from. A signal with no question is cost (section 12 prices it). A question with no signal is the next incident.
49e9c4a613:
Two of these rows deserve a sentence more, because exam scenarios lean on them.

Quality signals are proxies. You can't have a person grade every production answer. So you combine cheap behavioural signals, a sampled automated grader (chapter 11) and periodic human review. A sudden move in any of them is an event, not a verdict.

And "did something change" is the most valuable row and the cheapest: a string attribute on every span. Nearly every diagnosis in chapter 12 begins by splitting a metric by prompt version, model and index version. A team that didn't record them has to reconstruct the answer from deploy logs.
bc5928f546:
Every team should own one piece of code and review it like a security control: the wrapper through which every model call passes. It has four jobs.

  1. It opens a span with a fixed shape.
  2. It sets the attribution attributes from a context object, so no developer has to remember to pass a tenant identifier into a helper.
  3. It reads the usage object on the response, computes the cost from a versioned price table, and writes both onto the span.
  4. It records the metrics in process, so the counters are exact even when the traces are sampled.

Everything downstream (cost reports, dashboards, cache alerts, the replay set) is a query over what this one function emits. That also makes it the right place to enforce the privacy rule. Content never enters it, and only an explicitly enabled, redacted copy leaves it (section 15).
dd5ee1d529: The version below is written against the OpenTelemetry API for Python and the Anthropic SDK. The companion folder has a line-for-line sibling in obs.py that runs offline on a virtual clock. The span shape, attribute names and cost arithmetic are identical, which is why example 02 can check them.
6c5950396f:
Read the wrapper for its decisions, not its syntax.

Metrics are recorded where the response arrives, not derived later from traces. The trace store will be sampled (section 13); a counter must not be. A cost dashboard built from sampled traces is wrong by the sampling factor, and wrong in a biased direction.

The tenant appears twice, deliberately. The raw identifier is a span attribute, where unbounded values are cheap. Only the tier is a metric label, where they are expensive (section 11).

Content is absent. There's no prompt and no completion on the span. The only text-derived field is a length.

The model identifier comes from the response, not the request. The response says which snapshot actually served the call, and that's the only way to notice an alias moving.

And the price table has a version, stamped on every span. A cost computed in October stays explainable after a price change in January.
d07aeff55a:
Example 02 runs four calls through the offline sibling: a cache hit, a cache miss that writes the prefix, a provider 529, and a call that deliberately bypasses the wrapper. It then lints the spans for the required attributes and recomputes the cost of the first span by hand. Finally it compares the number of calls the client saw with the number of chat spans.

That last check is the cheap way to find the engineer who called the client directly. In a fleet of services, the gap between provider-side call counts and span counts is a coverage metric.
5aabcf3293: Note the 2.64 times. The miss costs more than two and a half times the hit. It writes 4,500 tokens to the cache at 1.25 times the input price, instead of reading them at one tenth. So whether a prompt is cached is one of the largest single influences on the cost of a call. That's why the cache-read and cache-write token counts are span attributes, not footnotes.
9ec24f711b:
Make the loop a parent span (invoke_agent) with app.agent.iterations and app.outcome attributes. Make each model call and tool call a child of it. Iteration counts then appear as a distribution you can alert on (section 24), not as an anecdote from an engineer who happened to open the right trace.

If you use the Claude Agent SDK, hooks around tool use are the natural place to open and close tool spans without touching tool code. Check the docs for the hook events and what each receives.
6d76b2482d:
The business services in the running example (the billing service, the plan catalogue) are Spring Boot applications. In many shops the agent service is too. Spring Boot 3 gives you HTTP server and client spans, Kafka spans and JVM metrics with no code. It does this through Micrometer Observation and Micrometer Tracing with an OpenTelemetry bridge (check the docs for the starter and exporter properties of your Boot version).

None of that covers the model call. The reason is the same as for any bespoke external system: the framework doesn't know the call is expensive, or that its response carries a token count. It needs explicit instrumentation.

The Spring-native way to write it is the Observation API. One of its features maps directly onto the cardinality discipline of section 11: low-cardinality key values become metric tags and span tags; high-cardinality key values go on the span only.
b3023562f4:
Three points for a Spring team.

First, the split into low- and high-cardinality key values is the architectural point. It makes the cardinality decision at the call site, where the developer knows what the value is. The alternative is a metrics-backend policy discovered after the bill arrives.

Second, the Observation API produces both the timer metric and the span from one definition, so the duration histogram and the trace can't disagree. Observation doesn't know about the token and cost counters, so those are recorded explicitly, and unsampled.

Third, a trace that crosses from the Python agent into a Spring service needs nothing from you if both sides use the W3C traceparent header. Both the OpenTelemetry Python instrumentation and Micrometer Tracing's OpenTelemetry bridge propagate it by default. Verify this on your versions in a staging environment; example 03 shows what happens when it silently doesn't.
57af774311: The line worth underlining is probability: 1.0. Sampling in the application is head sampling: the decision is made at the root, before anyone knows whether the request will fail or be slow. Exporting everything to a Collector tier and deciding there, after the trace is complete, is what makes tail sampling possible. Section 13 prices the buffer that requires. It's small.
57d73a514b:
A trace is only a trace if the identifier survives every hop. The agent calls the billing service over HTTP and the plan catalogue through an MCP transport. It also publishes a case event to Kafka for a downstream consumer.

At each boundary the sender must inject the W3C traceparent header (version, trace id, parent span id, flags) into whatever carries the request. The receiver must extract it and start its span as a child.

When one hop forgets, the failure is quiet. The downstream service still emits spans; they just belong to a different trace. The dashboard looks complete, and every trace is a fragment. Example 03 runs the same request with propagation off and on.
fb0a7d8c3f:
With propagation off, one user request produces four traces. There's the agent's root, with the two client spans and the producer span. Then there are three orphans, one each for the billing service, the MCP server and the Kafka consumer. Nothing errors.

A slow-request search finds the agent trace with a 410 ms gap in it. The 410 ms span that explains the gap sits in a different trace, and nobody connects the two. With propagation on there is one trace, and the critical path reads straight off the tree.
bc786bdfb0:
Three details matter at scale.

The sampled flag in traceparent carries the head decision downstream. A service that honours it keeps the whole trace or none of it. A service that makes its own decision tears traces in half. (With tail sampling the Collector decides after the fact, which is why the application exports everything.)

A malformed header must never fail the request. The receiver starts a new root trace and carries on, and a metric counts how often that happened. A rising count means some upstream is mangling the header.

And asynchronous hops need a deliberate choice. Picture a Kafka consumer processing a message minutes later. It should usually start a new trace and add a link to the producer's span, rather than parent under it. A trace that stays open for an hour is a trace the tail sampler can't decide on. The example parents the consumer span for simplicity; a production design chooses per topic.
c6b687d6f0: The same discipline applies to the attribution context: tenant, tier, feature, traffic class. The gateway or the first service sets it once, at the edge. It travels with the trace as baggage or an explicit context object, never as a parameter each developer must remember. The failure it prevents is the helper function, written in a hurry, that calls the model without a tenant. After that, a slice of spend belongs to nobody.
0073aa269f: Three kinds of telemetry are routinely confused. The confusion produces the two commonest design errors in this domain: rates computed from sampled traces, and prompts written to the application log. Each kind answers a different question, at a different cost, and relates differently to sampling and to privacy. The design gives each one its own pipeline.
65c840aa59:
The practical rule: answer rate and cost questions from metrics, causal questions from traces, evidence questions from the content store. Never use one as a substitute for another.

A tail-sampled trace store can't tell you the error rate; it will report fourteen times the truth, as example 06 shows. A metrics store can't tell you why a single request was slow. And a content store without access controls is a copy of your customers' conversations. The figure below shows the pipeline that follows from the rule.
6062ff575c:
A metrics backend stores one time series for every distinct combination of label values. It prices, caps or falls over on the number of series. A histogram adds one series per bucket on top: twelve buckets plus a sum and a count is fourteen series per label combination in the example.

The number of series is a product, not a sum. Adding one innocent-looking label multiplies the bill by the number of values it can take. A Spring architect has met this with Prometheus and Micrometer, where a userId tag on a timer is a classic outage. The arithmetic is the same here, with one new twist. The dimensions that make LLM cost attributable (model, tenant, feature, prompt version, token type) are exactly the ones that multiply.
3c6584491e: Example 04 prices five labelling schemes for a platform with three models, 40,000 tenants, twelve features, five live prompt versions and four token types. It measures them against an assumed allowance of 150,000 series and an assumed $8 per thousand active series per month. Both the allowance and the price are placeholders. The shape of the result is not.
6373bd0fe8:
Scheme A, every identifier as a label, comes to 129.6 million series and about $1.04 million a month in the example. That's within a factor of 1.2 of the entire inference bill from example 05. Scheme B, a user identifier as a label, is a thousand times worse; it's simply a way to crash the metrics backend. Scheme C replaces the tenant with its tier (five values) and lands at 16,200 series, a tenth of the allowance.

The decision that follows is the one the exam tests: put unbounded identifiers on spans, where each value costs one span attribute, and keep metric labels to bounded sets.
62881fe7ed:
The example also shows what happens at the cap, and that's worse than the bill. A backend or client-side guard that refuses new series doesn't raise an error. It drops the increments. With a cap of 500 series and 2,000 distinct users, 1,500 increments vanish. The dashboard shows only the first 500 users, with no hint that anything is missing.

So a cardinality problem shows up as quietly wrong numbers before it shows up as a large invoice. The defence is a metric on the metrics pipeline itself: the number of active series per metric name, with an alert at 70 percent of the allowance, plus a count of dropped data points that must be zero.
4fa1b5857f:
Finance still wants the top fifty tenants by spend, per day. Scheme D answers by putting tenant on the cost counter. That's 40,000 tenants times 12 features, or 480,000 more series: three times the allowance. Scheme E labels the cost counter with the forty largest tenants plus an "other" bucket, which adds 492 series.

The cleanest answer sidesteps the metrics store. Every request already carries its tenant and cost on the span, and the unsampled cost records feed a daily rollup into a table. "Which tenants cost the most" is a batch query over records, not a dashboard panel. Answer it where unbounded keys are cheap.
58ccc6a702:
Observability has a price. Leave it off the requirements card and you invite the argument that happens in every programme at the first budget review: the platform bill is a third of the model bill, and nobody can say which part is worth it.

Write the telemetry budget on the card as a share of inference spend (this chapter uses 5 percent). Price each design against it, and the argument becomes arithmetic.

The costs come in three lines, with different drivers:

  • trace ingest and storage (spans times bytes);
  • indexed content storage (bytes of text in a hot, searchable tier);
  • metric series (section 11).

Example 05 measures spans per request on the synthetic fleet and prices four capture designs at 2,000,000 requests a day.
6f0aea99ad:
Read the result against the 5 percent rule. Keeping every metadata-only trace costs about $10 a day against $40,280 of inference: 0.03 percent. Tail sampling to 6 percent cuts that to sixty cents. Capturing redacted content on the kept 6 percent adds a few cents, because it goes to cold storage.

Capturing content on every request into hot indexed storage costs $328 a day, or 0.81 percent. That's still inside the rule, and still the second-largest line. The metric-series line is the one that can exceed the inference bill: scheme A is 86 percent of it.

Look at the cheap, high-volume Haiku classifier at the bottom of the output, with a call that costs $0.0007. The same designs take a larger share there (1.74 percent for content everywhere). Telemetry cost scales with spans and bytes, while inference cost scales with tokens. A short classification has few tokens and a full set of spans.
3f495c44a4:
Three conclusions follow, and they invert the usual instinct.

First, the lever is what you store and which labels you emit, not whether you trace. Cutting the trace sample rate saves cents. Removing a label saves a million dollars. An engineer who answers "the observability bill is too high" by lowering the trace sample rate has attacked the smallest line.

Second, the economics change with the model tier and the price model. The numbers above rely on per-gigabyte pricing. A vendor that charges per span, per indexed log event or per host changes which line dominates. Run example 05 with your vendor's price list before arguing from it.

Third, the budget is a constraint that keeps the design honest in both directions. A team under the 5 percent rule can afford more telemetry than it thinks. Use that headroom to keep metadata tracing at 100 percent export and redacted content on a small sample, rather than sampling the traces themselves blind.
964df42a4d:
One agent request produces seven to fifteen spans. At 2,000,000 requests a day that's 14 to 30 million spans, tens of gigabytes before content. Keeping all of them is affordable in the example. But it's rarely what a team wants to pay for, and for a long retention it's never what they want to search.

So which traces do you keep? That depends on the question you'll ask of them. For an LLM system the traces you need most aren't a random sample. They're the errors, the requests that breached the SLA, the unusually expensive ones, the escalations and guardrail blocks, and the runaway loops. Add a small random baseline for comparison.
4076182205: Example 06 runs all three strategies over 120,000 synthetic requests. The requests contain real errors (0.44 percent), SLA breaches, expensive requests, guardrail blocks and runaway loops. The example prints what each strategy kept.
9f81d73f39:
Look at the printed memory sizing. At the peak hour's 200 requests a second and a 60-second decision wait, the collector holds 12,000 traces in flight. That's around 0.13 GB of span data at 1,500 bytes a span.

Tail sampling's reputation for being heavy comes from systems with much higher rates and longer waits. For this fleet it's a pair of small instances. The real operational cost is the routing requirement, not the memory.

The decision_wait has to exceed the longest trace you care about. That's one reason for the runaway guard in section 24: a loop that runs for ten minutes is a trace the sampler can't hold.
54e35bdc64:
An architect must state two consequences explicitly, because the exam tests them.

Do not compute rates from sampled traces. Keep every error and 2 percent of successes, and the error rate in the trace store is wildly inflated (14.7 times here). Error rate, cost and latency percentiles come from the unsampled in-process metrics. Traces explain the numbers; they don't produce them.

The evaluation sample is a separate, designed sample. For online quality scoring (chapter 11), draw a stratified sample by feature and segment from the content store. The tail-sampled set over-represents failures and under-reports quality by ten points or more (section 21 shows the effect).
268cb93afb:
And one limit. Some feedback arrives after the trace completes: a thumbs-down ten minutes later, or an escalation resolved the next day. It can't influence a decision made 30 seconds after the request. In the example, 7,859 requests receive a late thumbs-down.

Record such feedback as a separate event keyed by the trace id. Keep the content-store record by that key, under its own retention rule. Then the evidence for "the answer was wrong" is still there when the signal arrives.
5b66e7c12e:
A telecom assistant sees names, addresses, account numbers and the last digits of payment cards. It sees device identifiers (an IMEI is personal data in most privacy regimes) and call detail context. Now and then it sees a full card number that a customer typed into the chat because they thought it would help.

Every one of those can end up in a prompt, a tool result or a completion. From there it can reach a span event, a log line or an error message. The telemetry pipeline then holds a second, less controlled copy of the customer's data. That system has its own vendor, its own retention, its own access list and, usually, no deletion workflow.

That's the hazard. It's a design problem, not a configuration one, because a hundred engineers will add a hundred attributes over the next year.
d266bf7b89: The design principle is redact at the source, before export. Redaction in the Collector, or in the vendor's user interface, is a backstop, not a control. By then the data has crossed a network boundary, sat in an exporter queue, and possibly been written to a debug log. The rest follows from a short list of rules.
a9c7e0a5b1: Default off. Content capture is disabled for every feature. Spans carry token counts, lengths, hashes of identifiers, versions and scores. That's enough for latency, cost and most failure diagnosis.
cbaa82feff: An allow-list of attribute keys in the SDK. A span processor drops any key not on the list, and redacts every string value on the keys that are. This is the control that survives a developer writing span.set_attribute("prompt", text) at four o'clock on a Friday.
636fc1eb17: Pseudonymise identifiers with a keyed hash. Replace user and account identifiers with an HMAC whose key lives in the secret manager. Engineers can still group by user. Nobody can reverse the value without the key. Rotating the key breaks linkability on a schedule you choose. A plain unsalted hash of a 10-digit phone number isn't pseudonymisation: the space is small enough to enumerate.
85eadffdf4:
The Luhn check is the detail worth explaining. A card number is a 13 to 19 digit string whose last digit is a checksum. A regex for "long digit strings" alone would also redact order numbers, tracking numbers and every other long identifier in a telecom system, and the logs would become useless. Requiring the checksum to pass keeps most of them readable.

It isn't free. About one random 16-digit order number in ten is Luhn-valid by chance and gets masked as a card; example 07 measures this at 10.0 percent. Over-redaction is the safe failure. The cheap remedy is to give your own order identifiers a prefix the pattern doesn't match. Example 07 measures the redactor on 600 labelled synthetic messages.
9a921fbdd4:
The measurement is the honest part of the chapter. Structured identifiers (cards, phone numbers, emails, account numbers, SSNs, IMEIs) are removed 100 percent of the time in this set. None of the look-alikes is wrongly masked.

Names and street addresses are removed zero percent of the time. The last example in the before-and-after block shows why. "my daughter Priya Raman at 12 Elm Street cannot log in" contains no pattern. A named-entity-recognition model raises the recall on free text (open-source detectors exist; check the docs of whichever you evaluate). But it never reaches 100 percent, it adds latency, and it has its own false-positive rate.

The architectural conclusion is the one in rule 1. Free-text personal data can't be reliably removed, so the default is no text in telemetry. Any feature that captures text does so under a policy with a purpose, a sample rate, a retention and an access list. Redaction reduces the risk in the text you decided to keep. It doesn't decide whether to keep it.
706b697ded:
There are good reasons to keep some content. A sample of prompts and completions is the raw material for graded evaluation (chapter 11), for replay (section 23), and for diagnosing the failure that only shows up in the text.

What makes this safe isn't a clever redactor. It's a policy that states, per feature, whether capture is on, at what sample rate, for what purpose, for how long, and who may read it. A linter rejects policies a data-protection officer would reject. Write the policy as data in the same repository as the code. Then a change to it is a reviewed pull request with a diff, and the linter runs in the pipeline.
dbd43f6d89:
The lint in the example rejects a deliberately bad entry six ways: raw mode, no purpose, no access group, a one-year retention, a 100 percent sample, and a CPNI-bearing feature with capture on.

The second half pushes a span through the layers. With no layers, the canary card number and the raw customer id reach the backend. With the SDK allow-list alone, the raw prompt attribute is dropped, the card inside the error message is redacted, and the id is replaced by its pseudonym. With the Collector backstop alone, the same mistakes are caught, but only after they've crossed the network.

Why run both and assert on the result? Because the privacy requirement becomes a test. This script fails the build if the canary ever appears in the output.
e2355278b0:
Two operational notes. First, write the content store asynchronously from the request path, keyed by trace id. A slow store then never adds user-visible latency, and a failed write never fails the request.

Second, log access to the store itself. "The on-call engineer opened 40 conversations during that incident" is the kind of fact an auditor asks for. It's cheap to produce if the access log exists, and impossible to reconstruct if it doesn't (chapter 14).
7c868ffc86: Dashboards answer "what is happening". Alerts answer "does a person need to act now". The common failure is a catalogue of alerts on symptoms nobody can act on, which trains the on-call engineer to ignore the pager. SRE practice has the remedy: alert on the rate at which the error budget is being spent, not on the instantaneous value of a metric.
37c4a3069a:
Take the latency SLO of bill_explain from the card: 95 percent of requests complete within 7 seconds over 30 days. The budget is 5 percent of requests.

Define the burn rate over any window as the observed fraction of slow requests divided by the budget fraction. A burn of 1 spends the budget exactly at the end of 30 days. A burn of 6 spends it in five days. A burn of 2.4 (12 percent slow) spends it in 12.5 days.

The alert rule combines two windows. A long one makes sure the burn is real, and a short one makes sure it's still happening. That way a problem that has already stopped doesn't page.
fd4e78ad2c: Example 09 simulates one day at 1,800 requests a minute, with three events. It compares the rules with a static "p95 above 7 seconds" alert, which is the same as "slow fraction above 5 percent".
4eef0ebeb2:
Read the table in the output as the argument.

Event A is a three-hour regression at 12 percent slow, a burn of 2.4. It consumes 0.95 percent of the monthly budget. A static alert on the SLA wakes someone for 180 minutes over something the SLO says is affordable. The multi-window rules correctly do nothing. The ticket rule doesn't even fire, because the six-hour window never reaches 2x.

Event B, at 45 percent slow for an hour, consumes 1.23 percent of the monthly budget. This is the one the page should catch, and it does, nine minutes in.

Event C, a two-minute blip at 30 percent, consumes 0.03 percent and is correctly ignored.

The window lengths trade detection time against noise, and the example lets you move them. Shorten the page window to catch B sooner, and C pages too.
fa4e4665cf:
Burn-rate alerts suit the SLO-shaped signals: latency, errors, availability. Some GenAI-specific signals aren't SLO-shaped: cost per request, cache hit rate, escalation rate, iterations per request, quality. These are better served by relative-change alerts against a baseline. There's no contractual target to burn against; the target is "the same as last week".

Each alert in the catalogue below has a condition, a severity, an owner, a runbook and a first action. An alert missing any of the last three gets deleted, because nobody can act on it.
be1fd902e1:
A dashboard is justified by a decision a named person makes from it. The failure mode is the wall of forty panels that nobody owns and everyone consults during an incident. People find what they came for about half the time.

Five dashboards cover the platform, each with an audience and the question it settles. The release dashboard is the one that earns its place in chapter 12. Every panel on it can be split by prompt version or model, side by side, during a canary.
ae3eb4e364:
Two design rules keep these honest.

Show the denominator. A quality panel that says 91 percent without saying n = 46 invites a decision the data can't support. Example 13 shows how thin a random sample is for a feature with 10 percent of traffic.

And show the freshness. A panel built on a graded sample or a nightly rollup says when it was computed, so nobody treats Tuesday's number as Thursday's.
527ce64b95:
"The Claude bill went up 40 percent" isn't actionable. This is: "Feature bill_explain went from $0.022 to $0.043 per request after prompt be-v14, because cache-read tokens fell to zero". Cost attribution is the discipline of making that second sentence available within minutes of the change. It rests on three decisions, made once.

The attribution context is set at the edge. The gateway or the first service resolves tenant, tier, feature and traffic class and puts them in the trace context. Every model call reads them from there.

Cost is computed per call, from usage and a versioned price table. It isn't reverse-engineered from the monthly invoice. The table version is stamped on the span, so an October number stays explainable after a January price change.

And shared costs are allocated by a published rule. Some work serves no single tenant: the nightly re-embedding job, the evaluation runs, the shadow traffic. It's tagged to the platform, then either reported separately or allocated, for example in proportion to request share.
9e8281f34d: Example 10 reads 60,000 unsampled per-request records, including a prompt change that breaks the cache for one feature. It produces the six reports a finance conversation needs.
ef0313db31:
Report 1 is the release comparison. be-v14 costs 1.93 times be-v13 per request, and the cache hit rate falls from 64 percent to zero. The mix of tenants and traffic is the same, so the prompt is the cause.

Report 2 is the one product owners most often get wrong. The business unit is rarely a request. It's a resolved case, an answered contract question, a deflected call. Take a cheaper prompt that resolves 70 percent of cases instead of 82 percent. It's cheaper per request, but 65 percent more expensive per case once the escalations are priced ($1.25 against $0.76, with an assumed $4.10 for a human-handled escalation).

Report 5 is the quiet one. Ten percent shadow traffic replays each production call on two candidate prompts. Left untagged, it raises the apparent production cost per request by 5 percent and corrupts every quality panel it touches. The cure is one attribute, app.traffic = prod | shadow | eval, set by the wrapper and filtered by every dashboard.

Report 6 closes the loop with the invoice. A gap of a few percent between computed and billed cost is normal: rounding, token-counting differences, a price-table lag. A gap over about 3 percent is an investigation.
5dcbaba43a: Providers also publish their own usage and cost reporting. The Anthropic Admin API has usage and cost endpoints; check the docs for the current names, scopes and granularity. Use it as the reconciliation source, not the attribution source. It knows your organisation, workspace and API key. It can't know your features, tenants or prompt versions. A workspace per environment or per major feature is a cheap extra dimension on the provider side. The per-call numbers in your own telemetry fill in the rest.
cefc0306a0:
Prompt caching reuses the processing of an identical prefix of the prompt. Everything above the cache breakpoint must be byte-for-byte the same between requests for the cache to be read. The first character that differs ends the reusable prefix.

So the commonest incident in this domain is a harmless-looking edit that puts something volatile above the breakpoint. A timestamp in the system prompt ("Current time: ..."). The customer's name in the first line. A request identifier. A feature flag rendered into the tool descriptions.

Nothing breaks. Answers are identical. The cache hit rate falls from 65 percent to zero, and the cost per request roughly doubles. No error rate, status code or latency SLO notices, because a cache miss makes the call only somewhat slower but a great deal dearer (prefill instead of a cache read).
f771336936:
Two alerts detect it. They're cheap, because the data is already on every span: the cache hit rate dropping more than 20 points against a 7-day baseline, and USD per request rising more than 30 percent.

Example 11 simulates six hours with the deploy in the middle of hour 2. Both alerts fire in the first full window. Then the example does the diagnosis: render the system prompt for three consecutive requests and find the first position where the renders differ.
3c87c1d559:
The CI test that prevents it is four lines. Render the system prompt twice with different request identifiers, timestamps and customer names. Compute the common prefix. Fail the build if it's shorter than the portion you intend to cache. The test costs nothing to run and catches the incident at the pull request.

(The minimum cacheable prefix length and the way breakpoints are placed are model- and API-specific; check the docs. The example uses 1,024 tokens as an assumed minimum for illustration.)
5d33d67d95:
Situation. The bill_explain SLA is p95 end-to-end under 7.0 seconds and TTFA under 3.0 seconds. On Tuesday the latency burn-rate page fires: p95 is 7.7 seconds. The agent wasn't deployed today, the error rate is flat, and the provider status page is green.

The team has telemetry and nothing else. The exercise is to reach the cause using, at each step, the cheapest signal that narrows the hypothesis. Chapter 12 formalises that pattern.
ecc8fa4e91:
Step 1, scope with metrics. Split the duration histogram by feature, model and prompt version. Only bill_explain is affected, and all prompt versions equally. The model identifier returned by the API (gen_ai.response.model) is unchanged. Per-call TTFT is flat. So the prompt, the model and the prefill are exonerated. The extra time comes from somewhere else: more calls, or slower tools.

Step 2, look at the iteration distribution. The agent span records app.agent.iterations. Its p95 moved from 2 to 3 at a specific minute.

Step 3, compare per-span-name statistics before and after. This is a query over the sampled traces, and that's a legitimate use: you're comparing shapes, not computing rates. Per request, chat spans went from 2.00 to 3.00, and execute_tool get_plan spans from 1.00 to 2.00. The p95 duration of each individual span is unchanged. The request is slower because it does more, not because anything is slower.
951465f014:
Step 4, find the cause. Filter the slow traces to those whose get_plan span has status ERROR. The server attribute points at the plan-catalogue MCP server, owned by another team. Its spans, joined to ours through traceparent, show a new validation error ("region code required"). Their 09:30 deploy introduced it.

The model recovers correctly. It reads the error, adds a region, and calls the tool again. That's good behaviour, and it costs a full round trip, including a second send of the whole context.

Step 5, price it. Tokens per request rose 48 percent. Cost per request went from $0.0219 to $0.0307, a 40 percent increase on the feature, from an incident that never produced a user-visible error.
e1a80a5472:
Step 6, decide. In the short term, the catalogue team rolls the change back, or the tool wrapper fills the region from account context, which removes the round trip. In the medium term, add an alert on tool error rate per tool, owned by the tool's team (section 16). Add a contract test between the agent's tool schemas and the MCP server, so the validation change fails a build instead of a customer.

Changing the model or the prompt, the tempting first moves, would have helped nothing.

This is the CCAR-P answer to "what do you do first when latency regresses". Use the cheapest signal that narrows the hypothesis. Change nothing until you can name the cause. And check the cost side effect of the incident, not just the latency.
cf5f72bc8c:
Latency, cost and errors are mechanical, and you can measure them on every request. Quality is different. The system's most important failure, a fluent wrong answer, produces no event. So quality telemetry is built from three imperfect things.

Behavioural proxies are cheap, available on every request, and biased: escalation to a human, a re-ask within two minutes, a thumbs-down, a human agent overriding a draft. They tell you that something moved. They're noisy in the other direction too, since customers escalate for reasons unrelated to the answer.

A graded sample is expensive and accurate. An automated grader scores a sample of production answers for groundedness or correctness, and humans audit a smaller sample of the grader's judgements. Chapter 11 builds and calibrates the grader; here we only need the sample.

Replay (section 23) lets you answer "would the new prompt have done better on the cases that went wrong?"
c6c6a07c1d: This section exists to prevent one design error: grading whatever the trace sampler happened to keep. The tail-sampled set is full of failures by construction, so it under-reports quality. It also changes whenever a sampling policy changes, so trends in it are artefacts. Example 13 compares three estimates of groundedness against the truth on 90,000 synthetic requests, where quality is worse for escalated and thumbed-down requests.
43d981467c:
The tail-kept set reads 77.6 percent against a true 92.1 percent for bill_explain. That's a 14-point error, in the direction that triggers false alarms.

A simple random sample of 600 is unbiased but thin. It contains 46 contract_qa cases. The estimate for that feature (84.8 percent against 89.4) has an interval wide enough to hide a real 3-point drop.

The stratified sample draws within each feature and outcome stratum and weights by stratum size. It lands within a point or two for all three.

For planning, the sample-size calculation is the useful part. Detecting a 3-point drop in groundedness with 5 percent significance and 80 percent power takes roughly 1,350 graded cases per window for bill_explain (93 percent baseline), 1,060 for plan_advisor and 1,770 for contract_qa. A random sample that gives contract_qa 1,770 cases has to be 17,800 requests, since only ten percent of traffic is contract_qa. So the sample is stratified by feature, and the minority feature gets its own quota. These counts are what the grading budget in the cost model has to pay for.
0a7f8d10fe:
The final block shows why proxies are worth having despite their bias. With 40,000 escalation-eligible requests a week, a two-point rise in escalation rate (13.1 to 15.1 percent) has a z-score of 8. That's unmistakable, and it's available the same day with no grading.

The proxy says something moved. The graded sample says whether quality moved. The diagnosis in chapter 12 says why. You need all three, because each has a blind spot the others cover.
bd035e600f:
A model-backed feature can change while nobody ships anything. Drift comes in three kinds, and they differ in cause, detector and response.

Input drift is the questions changing. A device launch doubles activation questions. A billing-system migration changes the wording of invoice lines. Customers start pasting longer messages. The system isn't wrong yet. But the evidence you collected before (the evaluation set, the prompt's examples, the retrieval index) may no longer represent the traffic.

Output drift is the system's behaviour changing without an input change. A model alias moves to a new snapshot, a prompt template is edited in a database, a retrieval index is rebuilt.

Quality drift is the graded rate or a proxy moving, from either cause.

The detectors are small. The work is in choosing thresholds against the false-alarm rate you can afford, so example 14 measures each.
99f9f63ac9:
For input drift, the example uses the population stability index (PSI) on the daily intent mix against a reference week. The conventional bands are under 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 watch, and over 0.25 act. Over 200 stable days the maximum PSI is 0.0009, so false alarms at 0.10 are zero. A device-launch day (activation questions going from 14 to 27 percent of traffic) scores 0.114, a WATCH.

The lesson is in the next line. An ordinary Saturday scores 0.124 against a weekday reference, because the weekend mix is different. Seasonality looks exactly like drift unless the reference is the same weekday. Compare Saturday with Saturdays.

For output drift, the example uses the daily mean of output tokens against 30 stable days. A snapshot change that makes answers 25 percent longer is flagged on the first day, with no false alarms. You know which snapshot served each call from the gen_ai.response.model attribute the wrapper already records.

The general defence is to pin a dated snapshot rather than an alias, where the provider offers one. Treat a move of the alias as a change request with a replay run (section 23). How aliases and snapshot retirement work is provider policy, so check the docs for the current rules.
174543d665:
For quality drift, the example runs a one-sided CUSUM on the daily escalation rate: baseline 13.1 percent, shifting to 15.5 percent from day 31. With a slack of two standard deviations and a threshold of twenty, it raised no alarms in 300 stable 90-day runs. It caught the shift in all 300 shifted runs, with a median delay of 10 days.

Those 10 days are the price of zero false alarms on a daily sigma of 0.62 points. Loosen the threshold and the delay shortens, but alarms start appearing. A slice with a tenth of the volume has three times the sigma, so small features need weekly windows. The choice is a trade-off to state, not a setting to copy.
e4b09cf142: On an alarm, the response is procedural and the same for all three. Freeze the release train for the affected feature. Pull the graded sample (section 21). Compare gen_ai.response.model, the prompt version and the index version across the change point. Hand the result to the diagnosis in chapter 12. An alarm without that procedure is just a notification.
685f8a5ec8:
Replay is the bridge between observability and evaluation. Production traffic contains the cases that went wrong. An evaluation set (chapter 11) contains the cases somebody thought of. Re-run the real failures against a candidate prompt or model, with the tool results held fixed. That answers "would this change have fixed the cases that hurt us?" faster and more honestly than inventing new cases.

To do that, you must have recorded enough:

  • the template version and rendered-prompt hash;
  • the model identifier and the parameters;
  • the (redacted) messages;
  • the tool results as they were;
  • the retrieval document identifiers and index version;
  • the recorded answer;
  • a content hash, so a tampered bundle is detectable.

A bundle contains content, so it lives in the access-controlled content store under the policy of section 15. Bundles are selected from the sampled traces: the escalations, the thumbs-downs, the guardrail blocks.
ae0e0cfdba:
Three properties of replay are easy to get wrong.

First, tool results are stubbed from the bundle, not re-fetched. A bill "as of now" isn't the bill the customer saw. And a tool with side effects must never run against a live system in a replay.

Second, sampling makes the model non-deterministic. Replay the same configuration twice and you get different text, so a diff of text proves nothing. Example 15 measures the noise floor. Two replays of the same configuration agree on the text for 30 percent of cases, and on the pass/fail check for 88 percent. That's exactly what two independent 94-percent-accurate runs should do (0.94 squared plus 0.06 squared). Read any claim about a candidate against that floor.

Third, a replay set is a sample, so it needs an interval. With 80 cases, a candidate at 100 percent (95 percent interval 0.95 to 1.00) and the current prompt at 95 percent (0.88 to 0.98) can't be told apart. A regression to 85 percent (0.76 to 0.91), though, is clearly worse than a good candidate. Replay finds cases and rejects clear regressions. Confirmation comes from the graded evaluation set and a canary (chapter 12).
eca0cd6fc1:
An agent loop is a loop: it ends when the model stops asking for tools. Suppose a tool fails the same way every time and the model keeps retrying. The loop doesn't end until the context fills, and each iteration re-sends a longer history.

In the sketch of example 17, an unguarded loop makes 25 model calls, costs $1.09 and runs 45 seconds for one question. The same request with a guard stops at six iterations, costs $0.11, and returns a fallback in 10.8 seconds. The synthetic fleet injects runaways into 0.3 percent of 2,000,000 requests a day. That's 6,000 runaways a day and about $5,900 a day of avoidable spend.

A runaway loop is also a denial-of-wallet vector: a crafted input that provokes retries. So the guard is a cost control, a latency control and a security control in one.
1c2edce79c:
The guard is three budgets per request, enforced in the loop before the next model call: a maximum number of iterations, a maximum of total tokens, and a maximum wall time.

On breach, the loop stops and the user receives a safe fallback and a hand-off. The request records a span event and a counter with the reason. The tail sampler keeps it, because its outcome is budget_exceeded.

The telemetry that goes with it watches the distribution. Iterations per request is a histogram, with an alert when its p99 reaches the cap and a page when any request hits the cap.

The cap is a design number. Set it from the p99.9 of healthy traffic plus a margin: healthy bill_explain needs two or three iterations, and the cap here is six. Review it when a new tool is added.
0f1ec29852:
An alert catalogue is software, and like software it can be tested. The tests are the incidents you already know about. For each one, replay its telemetry through the rules and assert which alerts fire and how long after the start.

Example 16 does this with three incidents injected into the synthetic fleet: a cache break, the MCP validation change, and runaway loops. It runs them against the catalogue of section 16, expressed as data: condition, severity, owner, runbook, first action. First it lints the catalogue, rejecting any alert with no owner, runbook or first action. Then it measures false alarms on a clean day. Then it replays each incident in 10-minute windows.
ae8924f84c:
Three results are worth reading closely.

The clean day has zero false alarms across 40 windows. That's the precondition for anybody trusting a page.

The cache incident is caught by the two ticket-severity alerts (cost per request and cache hit rate), and by nothing that pages. That's by design. A cache regression costs money but doesn't breach an SLA, so the response is a ticket the same day.

The MCP incident is caught by five alerts at once: two pages (the latency SLOs) and three tickets (cost, iterations, tool error rate). That's the correct shape. The page tells the on-call engineer a customer-visible target is breached. The tickets point at the tool and its owner.

If an incident in your history would have been caught by nothing, you've found the next alert to write.
2ed65a7ea0:
Telemetry that touches personal data inherits the obligations of the data: a retention period, an access list, and a way to honour a deletion request. Chapter 14 covers the regimes (GDPR, HIPAA, FedRAMP, and in telecom CPNI and the rules around call-record data). The retention numbers in this section are placeholders for your counsel's answer.

The architect's job here is to make the answer cheap to implement. The cheapest implementation is to have designed the stores so there's little to find. Three stores, three rules.
35202825ce:
The erasure works because of one design choice made earlier. The user identifier in every trace is an HMAC pseudonym. So the content store can keep an index from pseudonym to the traces that hold content for that subject. Without the index, an erasure request is a full scan of a store designed for write throughput. With it, it's a lookup.

The verification step searches the stored text for the raw identifier, the card number and the email address, and finds none. The audit record states what was deleted (two content rows) without containing any of it.

The retention sweeps show a legal hold working. A guardrail-block record survives the 30-day sweep because it's held for 90 days, and it goes at the 91-day sweep.

The last block shows what key rotation does. Yesterday's pseudonym and today's can't be joined. That limits linkage across periods, but it also breaks long-running per-user analyses. So the rotation period is a decision with a stated trade-off, not a default.
13674c223c: Put the pieces together and ask the CCAR-P question: what is the simplest architecture that meets every line of the card? The answer has six components, and each exists because a requirement names it. There's no vendor on the diagram. The vendor is a procurement decision, and the architecture must survive it changing.
902b0c6a5e: The wrapper and the SDK guard (in every service). One function for every model call (section 07), an attribute allow-list that drops anything not on it (section 14), and in-process counters and histograms. Requirements served: cost, tokens, latency, privacy at the source.
a3ad86e90e: A Collector tier. It receives OTLP, applies a second redaction and hashing pass, tail-samples with the policies of section 13, batches, and exports. It's a backstop for privacy and the place where sampling decisions are made. It needs load balancing by trace ID, so one instance sees a whole trace. Requirements served: retain 100 percent of errors, SLA breaches, expensive requests and blocks, and stay inside the cost budget.
0f0185d1b6: A content store: off for contract_qa, and a 2 percent redacted sample for bill_explain. It has 30-day retention, role-based access, an index from pseudonym to rows, and replay bundles. Requirements served: quality grading (ch 11), replay, erasure (ch 14).
59f13e0251:
Three simplifications are worth defending, because the exam rewards them.

One wrapper, not a framework per team. A shared function and a lint that finds bypasses is lighter than an instrumentation library with plug-ins.

One Collector tier, not a sidecar per service. The tail sampler needs a whole trace in one place, so a central tier is required anyway. Sidecars add operational cost without adding that.

One content store, not content on spans. Text in span attributes is copied to every store the span reaches, and erasure becomes a multi-store problem. A separate store keyed by trace ID and pseudonym keeps it a single-store one.
3a830f8b02:
What the diagram deliberately lacks answers the common wrong turns.

  • There's no streaming pipeline that re-parses logs into metrics, because the metrics are recorded at the source.
  • There's no per-user dashboard, because the user is a trace query, not a metric.
  • There's no "AI observability" platform in the critical path. Every requirement above is met with the standard stack. If the organisation wants an LLM-specific viewer, it subscribes to the same OTLP stream.
c18a07f70a: An architecture decision record for observability is short, and every line is a number from this chapter. It's also the artefact that survives the reorganisation, after which nobody remembers why traces are sampled. The record below is for the platform in the running example. All figures are the companion's synthetic or illustrative values, so replace them with measurements before you present it.
86462d7845: Notice what the ADR gives the next reader: a rejected option with its price, a sentence per number on where it came from, and review triggers that say when the decision stops being right. A reviewer can attack any line. Every line has an example in the companion that reproduces it.
98310757b7: Telemetry is code, and code that only incidents exercise is untested. Almost every property in this chapter can be tested in CI, against a fake client and an in-memory exporter, with no collector and no vendor. Five tests earn their place.
0bc10113ac:
For a Spring service, the same tests are JUnit tests. They use an in-memory span exporter (OpenTelemetry's SDK testing module provides one; check the docs for the artefact name in your version) and a stub implementation of the gateway interface.

Some arithmetic must be identical in Python and Java, and it's worth pinning with a cross-language test. A price or burn-rate formula that differs by a rounding rule produces two dashboards that disagree. The companion's Java file does this for the cost of a call, the burn rate, the page rule, and the parsing of a traceparent. It uses only the JDK, so it runs without a build tool.
8309701b4f: The alert replay test deserves a further note. Once an incident is understood, the last step of the post-incident review is to add its telemetry to the replay set and assert that some alert fires. Every outage then becomes a regression test for the alert catalogue, and the catalogue stays honest as it grows.
